The objects of such publications, as issue from
the newspaper press, doubtless, are twofold, and
no more:


First, to present in summary important and
interesting events and easily to be a medium
through which to educate, instruct, and persuade
the mind.


Accordingly papers have before them the broad
field of the world from which to gather facts
that are desirable to be known, and the equally broad
field of human thought to gather instruction and
life for the mind.


To accomplish their work more perfectly, and
to meet the distinct demands of the mind the
work of gathering and selecting—of unfolding and
impressing is divided. One class of periodicals
takes what pertains properly to the business
affairs of men—the affairs and relations of civil
society. The other chiefly confines itself to the fields
of morals and religion. These two distinct pro
vinces are properly separated and treated of in
different paper, and both are far more success
fully surveyed and the matters of each more full
ly discussed and presented, in this way, than they
could be if both fields and both objects were uni
ted in one.

what are termed religion papers in distinction
from those which are secular.

comparison of the relative importance of these
two kinds of papers. They are both necessary,
and this is enough now.


No man can be thought to be rational, in the
highest sense of the word, who neglects to ac-
quaint himself with what pertains to the moral,
intellectual, and spiritual condition of mankind.
